title: A hard state?
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
THESE days we are repeatedly told that the Pakistani state has been soft on anarchy for far too long. This is the considered and stated position of many state officials as well as of many supporters of those in power. Common people may hold any number of positions that one finds distasteful but the same sentiments being voiced by those in power invite both scrutiny and concern.
For the last three years, there has been much chatter about turning Pakistan into a ‘hard state’. No one has given an adequate definition of what this entails, but based on disparate statements and impulses, we can gather this has something to do with protecting the rights of the state and the decision-makers who staff it. These rights are being obtained via a frequently violent trade-off with the rights of the people of Pakistan. 
The projected consequence of such a trade-off is that protest of all shades becomes a privilege. Demands can only be voiced with due approval through vetted content and NOCs. Speech is to be regulated via defamation, criminalisation laws, and an apparently pliant judiciary till it takes on an acceptable hue, or preferably till it becomes an echo of the state’s.
These impulses are neither unique to the Pakistani state nor are they exceptional to this current moment. Trysts with authoritarianism dot the country’s past and arguably lie at the roots of its state structure. British viceregal authority bequeathed an overdeveloped administrative apparatus, which has since then done exceedingly well to reproduce itself and the privileges of those who staff it. When given a chance, politicians of nearly all stripes — centralists, federalists, provincial magnates, or constituency-level bigwigs — have been more than happy to fortify this arrangement for their own and their clients’ benefits.
And yet there is a question that should gnaw at anyone who thinks about the trade-off at the table. What is all of this for? If people are being asked to voluntarily or otherwise forfeit their constitutional or social rights, it only makes sense to interrogate what end goal this forfeiture is designed to serve.
Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve?
Forfeiture of individual liberty is commanded by all states in service of some basic objectives. Usually the foremost of these objectives is territorial sanctity: no state tolerates geographic loss and will usually strip people of their rights, property and lives to prevent it. The Pakistani state is fairly typical in this manner. It deals with separatism/secessionism the way many other post-colonial states do, and with variable degrees of success. The bigger question on that front then is whether its strategy for preventing the rise or growth of this factor is useful at all.
Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Other states offer different types of answers. The case of China — paradigmatic for the 21st century — has a very simple one. It places limits on various forms of individual rights for the protection and promotion of the CCP’s endeavours. The main endeavour, since the 1970s at least, has been the growth and collective prosperity of the Chinese people via the unleashing of productive forces (labour and capital), both by the state and by private enterprise. The state under one-party rule decides the degree of this unleashing, its objectives, and ultimately the distribution of its fruits.
In the previous century, socialist states decided that the true fulfilment of human life lay in getting rid of privatised forms of exploitation. And so a suspension of individual liberty was done in service of collective ownership of resources, commandeered by the state. Social democratic states in Western Europe decided to infringe on the rights of capital owners over their profit in order to redistribute benefits to the working class via taxation. The late-20th-century Asian Tigers took away social rights of the working poor to generate double-digit capitalist growth.
There are other, less palatable answers too. The fascists in Germany stripped the rights, property, and lives of one minority group and various ideological dissenters (primarily the communists) in service of its ethnonationalist and expansionist agenda. At present, the ruling party in India targets individual liberties of specific segments, such as Muslims, to fulfil the cultural agenda of its majority base.
In all of these examples, the use of state power is for some larger agenda; a larger agenda in the name of the public (or at least an important part of it), built on specific ideational values and postulates. Something being done in service of something bigger, grander, and to varying degrees, collective.
So one must pose the question: what objective does this particular, three-year-old vintage of the ‘hard state’ serve in Pakistan?
To date there is no coherent answer. We do not know what the killing of protesters — regardless of the agreeability of their demands — in AJK is going to achieve. What goal banning political movements in the peripheries serves. What Form-47ing election outcomes does. What the hollowing out of the opposition, judiciary, media or civil society helps obtain.
If the answer is to maintain territorial integrity, then the vast majority of those whose rights stand stripped away carry no geographic ambitions. If the answer is to unleash GDP growth rates of the kind unseen in the last two decades, then one must reluctantly point out that the needle is yet to move up at all. If the answer is to project sovereignty and stature on the world stage at a time of global upheaval, the logical follow-up is a) whose stature and b) sovereignty in whose name?
There are no ready grand answers at the end of this line of inquiry because there is likely no grand thought among those steering the ‘hardening’. The actual answers, if one were to hazard a guess, are probably several degrees more modest: the prolonging of duration in office, an improvement in personal quality of life, and the distribution of gifts and sinecures to a small coterie of loyalists at the expense of everyone else. 
The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.

title: Urban flooding
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE warning from the disaster management and weather authorities that a new monsoon spell could trigger urban flooding in major cities across Punjab and Sindh is yet another reminder of how poorly prepared our cities are for heavy rainfall.
Cities from Rawalpindi, Lahore and Multan in Punjab, to Hyderabad, Umerkot and Tando Allahyar in Sindh, have been flagged for urban flooding. This is not unusual during the monsoons. However, what makes this year’s warning worth pausing on is the Met Office’s forecast of below normal rainfall this year. Still, less rainfall will not eliminate the risk of flooded cities if a burst of rain arrives faster than the ground and drains can carry it away. This says more about the state of our cities than about the weather.
The problem of urban flooding in Pakistan is no longer limited to low-lying neighbourhoods. It has become a structural feature of how the country has grown and urban centres have developed. Unplanned construction has taken place over drainage channels and wetlands that once absorbed rain. Waterways have been encroached upon, storm-water systems are built for outdated rainfall patterns, and drains are choked with solid waste that no longer has any place to go.
    
The response is reactive across the provinces. Drains are cleared only when the rain starts to fall; pumps arrive after roads are under water; and warnings are issued, repeated, then forgotten until the next spell. This is crisis management dressed up as preparedness. Most Pakistani cities have no comprehensive flood-risk maps, no functioning drainage master plans, and no clear chain of command for who acts first as the water rises. Drainage, roads, water supply and disaster response sit in separate departments that rarely coordinate before a flood and mostly trade blame after one.
Climate change has broken the old planning assumptions. Cities now need infrastructure built for short, intense downpours capable of overwhelming drains within minutes, not the gradual rainfall patterns those systems were designed around decades ago. Every new road, housing scheme or commercial project should be assessed for how it disrupts the natural water flow before approval, not after the damage becomes visible. Existing drains need redesigning and expanding to match current rainfall intensity, rather than being patched up just before the monsoon.
    
Pakistan cannot control how much rain falls. But it can control the extent to which the rain turns into a disaster. The recent warning is not a new problem; each year, governments assure the public that they are ready for the rains. Unfortunately, the very first intense downpour exposes their claims. What the country needs is sustained investment in drainage infrastructure and local governments to maintain it between the monsoons, not just during the rainy season.

title: Power and youth
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
YOUTH are highly innovative in expressing their anger. Meanwhile, ruling elites struggle to understand that the existing power structure can no longer meet the aspirations of the young. The context of this statement is neither the events in Delhi, where the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) succeeded in achieving its demands, nor the violent protests in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, nor the recent provocative statement by the federal interior minister about the state system. Rather, the reference is to a silent protest by the youth of Khuzdar in Balochistan, in which they succeeded in having their demand met. Is it not a unique event in Pakistan when the demands of the youth are met?
What was the youth’s demand? The reopening of a local library, where students study and prepare for their civil service examinations. The library was closed by the local bureaucracy, quite likely with the consent of superior institutions, which see books and libraries as sources of dissent. One cannot spare the bureaucracy either, which has a narrow vision and has been taught to rule like colonial masters. There is a high probability that in Khuzdar, too, they would have seen the youth’s inclination towards books and literature as a potential threat to security. It is ironic that most students, including many female students, were using the library as a safe and peaceful space to prepare for their exams. Most of them aspired to become bureaucrats, but the bureaucracy itself had shut down the library and closed the door to their future.
    
Whatever factors were involved in the library’s shutdown, the youth adopted a unique and peaceful way to protest. They held a sit-in outside the library and converted the footpaths and adjoining street into an open-air study space. They did not raise any slogans or attempt to confront the police or the local administration; they simply continued sitting silently and studying. Finally, the Balochistan chief minister intervened, and the library doors opened again.
This peaceful protest happened in a conflict-torn province where an insurgency is at its peak. The state has cracked down on violent actors. Sadly, those who participate in peaceful political and civil rights movements are also targeted. The district of Khuzdar has its own complex local, tribal and political context, and sardars, good or bad, have made the local people’s lives miserable. Yet the youth found a way to register their protest.
The youth are not politically blind; they see how the system works and how it is manoeuvred.
The protests by the youth in Khuzdar and by the CJP in India were related to education and inspired by the idea of getting a fair chance in life. Power structures have lost sight of the fact that equal opportunities and a fair system are essential for the youth. The youth are not politically blind; they see how the system works and how it is manoeuvred.
Whether it is referred to as Gen Z or Alpha-Z, this is a different generation with a different worldview. A dominant trend, especially among the more privileged youth of this generation, is to try out new modes of production and expand their class influence. Their forefathers accumulated leverage for their protection through wealth and relationships within the power structure. Less privileged youth are becoming less interested in civil services and industries and more interested in the corporate and financial sectors.
    
Certainly, the majority still belong to the middle- and lower-income groups, and they try every avenue they believe can empower them. They know that power is the only pathway to economic prosperity. Civil services and public-sector jobs of any sort are their shortcuts to finding a way out.
When someone tries to block the path to their dreams, they resist and protest. The older generations respond to the new generation in the conventional way, claiming that the new generation knows nothing. Where the youth have brought about political change, as in Nepal and Bangladesh, senior figures in the system dislike them and see their worldview as flawed.
A crisis is unfolding in Pakistan, particularly for the country’s youth. A draconian shift is taking place in the world of politics, where the older generation of politicians is transferring its legacy, power, and values to the next generation — not through legitimate constitutional and political means, but through shady deals with the most powerful. This process is occurring in every party, and the transition is frightening because those to whom power is being transferred have very little connection with political processes. They believe they are chosen to rule and can do anything to retain power. The youth of the country, then, has nothing to be proud of or to be inspired by in the existing political order.
This piece is not meant to predict any Gen Z-style uprising in Pakistan, but to point out that the political structure has become so tarnished and corrupt that it cannot sustain the burden of the economy, create new economic engines, or effectively utilise the existing sources of wealth. The bureaucratic structure is incapable of running governance and is becoming increasingly ruthless. A sense of deprivation is a common thread among young people from the middle- and lower-income classes.
Those in power are unwilling to review their practices; instead, they believe in an authoritarian, hegemonic style of controlling the system, in which subjects are expected to behave and follow whatever those in power dictate. The concept of citizenship was eroded long ago, and those who are powerless are treated merely as subjects. If they protest and their demands are fulfilled, they must consider themselves lucky, be thankful to the powerful, and forget that their success has anything to do with their ability to express themselves differently.
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, August 2nd, 2026

title: Not the right questions
author: none@none.com (Ghazan Jamal)
content:
BUDGET season is behind us — and with it the opportunity for productive conversations and comparisons centring on inter-governmental development priorities and structural reforms. In recent memory, the only time such conversations flooded the airwaves was after the KP chief minister’s visits to Lahore and Karachi some months ago. For a brief moment, comparisons between the progress achieved under the PTI’s 12-year rule in KP and the track record of parties in other provinces dominated the political discourse — from street discussions among residents to heated arguments between party leaders on national programmes. Given the divisive political slurs that normally eclipse serious political discussions, the debate on actual governance and performance was indeed a welcome change. How­ever, that is where the positivity ended. While greater insight may elude the man on the street regarding service delivery and development, the questions and responses of policymakers, elected officials and senior anchorpersons leave much to be desired. This is particularly apparent during the budget season — in the days leading up to its announcement and immediately after the document is released. It was no different this year.
For example, discussions on the education sector’s performance tended to focus on the number of new university buildings inaugurated. Elementary and secondary education were too ‘unimportant’ to even mention. This is ironic, considering that the government is constitutionally mandated to provide education to every citizen from ages five to 16. One would have hoped to see greater commentary on important aspects such as the progress made on increasing literacy rates and reducing the number of out-of-school children, improving test scores, fund allocation at the primary and secondary levels, and university admissions. Rather than listen to long-winded discussions on expensive infrastructure development at the higher education level, one would have preferred detailed analyses on the total number of graduates and how many of them were absorbed into the labour force, academic research and publications, university affordability, the financial status of public universities and their national and international rankings. These are crucial factors; unfortunately, the performance of many public universities has worsened on these fronts. Discussions on the topic could have exposed the government’s lethargy and challenged policymakers to do better. 
To assess various parties’ records on healthcare, the debate took a similar track, with party spokespersons essentially focused on naming large or tertiary-level hospitals inaugurated during their tenure. Emphasising expensive, specialised care is a misguided and wasteful approach in a country where the overwhelming majority of preventable deaths are due to causes that are treatable at the basic healthcare facility level or through improvement in public health efforts. The latter include better sanitation and vaccination outreach as well as behavioural changes. In Pakistan’s context, focusing the discussion on plans to increase the number of hospital beds, doctors and paramedic staff, improve access to basic healthcare, and keep healthcare affordable would be a better yardstick for comparing provincial performances. What is also left out is key health data, such as trends in mortality, disease and infection rates, and immunisation coverage. In a country where over 40 per cent of children under the age of five are affected by stunting (a consequence of poor hygiene and malnourishment), it was disappointing not to have comparisons focus on improvements in WASH and nutrition.
Similarly, there was little discussion on countering inflation and poverty. A recent report on poverty rates presents a damning picture: poverty rates have been increasing in all the provinces over the last few years. The other key economic concern for citizens is unemployment. Again, conversations about government interventions to lessen unemployment or about provincial enterprises and industrial policies, or even about boosting growth in general, never really got off the ground. This exposes the disconnect between broadcasters and policymakers and the issues that most affect people’s lives. It would have been very instructive for the public to hear informed conversations about these issues as well.
In at least two of the provinces, KP and Balochistan, security has become one of the biggest concerns for the public. Yet the debate arou­­nd the issue has focused more on jurisdictional disputes rather than actual efforts to ensure security. It is true that both the federal and provincial governments have a role to play in maintaining security, but constitutionally policing is strictly a provincial subject. Yet, rather than discuss interventions that have improved or aim to improve policing through better training, prosecutorial success, community engagement, equipment upgradation and other programmes, the parties were only keen to deflect responsibility — with not enough pushback from the anchorpersons. 
A more honest political discourse focused on crucial issues is needed.
Worst of all, there has been little conversation about key legislation passed. Often, there is criticism that parliamentarians are more interested in development work than legislation; yet the legislative output of their respective parties, and how it determines their performance, is hardly discussed. Perhaps the only exception is the citing of the 18th Amendment by the PPP and ANP. While this may be seen as a joint accomplishment by the provinces, surely political representatives can be asked to explain the performance of their respective provincial government and how it measures up to the policies made or the laws passed. Indeed, the policies and laws themselves are a point of discussion to see how far they go in promoting (or restricting) democratic norms.
Pakistan’s political discourse will benefit from more evidence-based third-party evaluation of provincial governments’ performances across all sectors over the past couple of decades. This will not only help foster healthy competition between the parties and their governments, but, more importantly, it will create an atmosphere of cross-province learning and best practices. A more honest political discourse focused on the right issues among party spokespeople and policymakers would contribute greatly to the designing and implementation of programmes to make Pakistan more prosperous. The first step to inculcate such a constructive atmosphere begins by asking the right questions.
The writer is a development practitioner and a former parliamentarian.

title: Dirty data centres
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
ABOUT a week ago, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif inaugurated what is billed as Pakistan’s largest data centre. The 8.5 MW facility is the creation of Sky47 AI Cloud, which is also reported to be constructing a slightly smaller 5 MW data centre at Karachi’s Port Qasim. According to speeches made at the event, the data centres are intended to provide the hard infrastructure for Pakistan’s artificial intelligence needs. 
There is no doubt that the world is clamouring to build data centres. In the US, industrial developers are buying up cheap rural land to locate massive data centres there. The biggest one, planned for a rural county in Utah, is intended to be some three times the size of Manhattan. Initial plans showed it at 40,000 acres, but after a Utah lawmaker pushed to shrink that footprint by three quarters, it shall be completed over 10,000 acres. It is expected to draw 7,000 to 9,000 MW. It is also expected to decimate climate and plant life around it: one estimate published as the project drew opposition suggests it could raise nighttime temperatures nearby by several degrees, killing plant and animal life in the area. Residents unlucky enough to live around it worry they could be left short of water and have to put up with the constant hum of thousands of fans cooling the mega computers inside.
Obviously the data centre inaugurated in Pakistan is a tiny baby compared to the behemoths being built in the US. However, now that Pakistan is eager to line up in the data centre queue, Pakistanis should know a few things about such massive infrastructures sprouting up quite literally overnight all over the world. We need data centres, of course, because we use AI. Free versions of products like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude are available online for nearly everyone to use. One widely cited study found that a full back-and-forth conversation of 20 to 50 questions with an early version of ChatGPT — anything from the best recipe for biryani to an explanation of the Pythagorean theorem — consumed the equivalent of roughly 500ml of water to cool the servers producing the responses. Now multiply that one bottle by the millions of such conversations held with AI in a single day. 
That is only the water demand — which in a country like Pakistan, already struggling to provide water for its humans, is a very pertinent one. In Karachi, where large swathes of the tens of millions go without water even in extreme heat, the question is even more crucial. At the inauguration, the prime minister noted that worldwide demand for data centres was an opportunity for Pakistan. Undoubtedly, the intention behind that desire — Pakistan providing technological infrastructure for the world — is a noble one. But if so much of the country, Karachi in particular, is in such dire straits over water, then imagining a data centre boom seems at least a little problematic. 
Who pays the price when power and water are diverted to computers?
Besides the water issue, data centres also put incredible pressure on electricity grids because of their massive demand. Currently, the largest electrical grid in the US is struggling to meet the data centres’ demand. Earlier this week, PJM Interconnection announced it would have to cut power to data centres during periods of shortage. PJM’s cuts, which apply only to data centres of 50 MW or larger, come as electricity demand from data centres is projected to increase at least fourfold within a decade. PJM is running an auction for power generating capacity. 
None of this makes the Pakistan inauguration a bad thing, nor is it wrong for the prime minister to voice optimism about the country’s technological future. But it is crucial to reckon with the demands these centres will make. Before Pakistan puts its name in the hat as a fu­­t­ure data centre hub, it is worth asking what investments could expand the country’s power generation capacity — and in a country of shortages, who pays the price when power and water are diverted from human to computer use. 
AI feels like magic: the power of insanely powerful computers at one’s fingertips, ready to answer even the most arcane questions. Ask ChatGPT the weather in Rome in 1275, then its take on zodiac compatibility; a few dozen questions like those are enough to empty a 500ml bottle’s worth of cooling water. 
It is commendable that Pakistan is building infrastructure for its technological future. It would be even more impressive if equal attention were given to the challenges that come with building it. The advancement of some Pakistanis should not come at the cost of further suffering for others already starved of water and electricity. 
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

title: Exchange rate dilemma
author: none@none.com (Farooq Arby)
content:
FEW economic issues provoke as much debate in Pakistan as the effect of the exchange rate on exports and the effectiveness of monetary policy when inflation is driven by supply-side factors. For now, we’ll focus on the nexus between the exchange rate and exports. While export-led growth remains a popular theme in policy discussions, an anti-export bias persists in practice. Unsurprisingly, despite decades of repeated policy failures, our approach to managing balance-of-payments remains unchanged. Policymakers have yet to accept that a market-based exchange rate and foreign exchange liberalisation are essential ingredients of a successful export strategy.
Two arguments are usually made to downplay the role of the exchange rate. The first is that the rupee has lost considerable value over the past several years, yet exports have remained stagnant. The second is that Pakistan’s export industries rely heavily on imported raw materials, meaning that currency depreciation increases input costs and thus dilutes any competitive gains.
Export growth critically depends on competitiveness, ie, the ability to produce and sell goods and services in international markets at prices and quality that outperform competitors. The determinants of competitiveness can broadly be divided into two categories: price factors and non-price or structural factors. Among the price factors, the real effective exchange rate is the most widely used measure of competitiveness. Maintaining a sound REER is important not only for exports but also for overall external-sector stability. A prudent policy, therefore, allows the nominal exchange rate to adjust over time to offset inflation differentials with trading partners and ensure a broadly stable REER.
Pakistan, however, has often followed the opposite approach. Instead of allowing the nominal exchange rate to reflect economic fundamentals, policymakers attempt to keep it artificially stable while allowing the REER to rise. As the Punjabi poet Ustad Daman said: “Iss jag di ulti ganga vich/ Phul dubda, pathar tarda ae” (‘In this world with river Ganga running upside down; the flower sinks, while the stone floats’). It is a great metaphor for how good things suffer and bad things prevail in a system.
Policymakers try to keep the exchange rate artificially stable.
The State Bank reports REER data on its EasyData portal, which is publicly accessible. An empirical analysis, using data covering the past five decades and controlling for inflation and real GDP growth, finds that an increase in the REER is followed by weaker export performance and a deterioration in the trade balance. By contrast, nominal depreciation of the currency improves the trade balance mainly by compressing imports. The estimated models explain more than 50 per cent of the variation in the trade balance ratio. The evidence, therefore, suggests that both the real and nominal exchange rates have considerable explanatory power for the trade balance. This is not merely a suggestion by exchange rate zealots.
Regarding imported raw materials, it should be noted that this is not something specific to Pakistan’s export sector. Modern manufacturing throughout the world is characterised by global value chains. Imported components are an integral part of export production in almost every country. That said, it is important to consider the dynamics of the imported input cost channel for export competitiveness.
Global increases in the dollar prices of imported inputs affect all competing producers with similar cost structures and comparative advantages, making such shocks broadly neutral from a competitiveness standpoint. Likewise, when the rupee depreciates, it simultaneously raises the local cost of im­­p­orted inputs and the rupee value of export recei­p­­ts. This dual ef­­fect implies that exporters’ net pro­fit margins may remain broadly un­­changed. Thus, the cost of imported inputs may not significantly affect export competitiveness; rather, domestic factors, including energy costs, taxes, regulatory burdens and other non-price considerations, play a more decisive role.
The exchange rate debate, however, extends beyond exports. An artificially overvalued currency renders imports cheaper, thereby putting pressure on the trade balance, and distorts resource allocation across the economy. It also suppresses the rupee value of legal remittances inflows, while benefiting illicit financial flows, including money laundering.
The lesson is straightforward. Exports certainly need enhanced productivity, logistics, technological sophistication and institutional quality, yet these must be complemented with a competitive exchange rate. A country that aspires to build an export-driven economy must first allow its currency to discover its true price. 
The writer is an economist.

title: Murders in Balochistan
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
GOOD news is scarce in Balochistan. Seven labourers were abducted and gunned down in Turbat city recently. Four belonged to Punjab and two to KP, suggesting that their ethnic background made them targets. Terrorist outfits have not just attacked politicians, activists and jurists, but also innocent non-Baloch workers who travel to the province in search of livelihoods. The killings of citizens must be unequivocally denounced, and the frequency and intensity of such attacks should set off alarm bells across the country and within the security apparatus. What the victims reflect is a deep insecurity driven by conflict and deprivation in the province.
Political disputes, ethnic turmoil and terrorism have left a resource-rich land poor and far behind the rest of Pakistan. Years of neglect, poverty and violence have created a gulf between the people and the state. With a fragile security situation, workers from other provinces often find themselves in a risky situation where varied power dynamics turn them into targets. Labourers across the country, irrespective of where they are working, deserve the same safety, rule of law and justice, and those killed should not become mere statistics. Such atrocities do nothing for Balochistan’s cause or for the rightful demands of its people. They simply perpetuate volatility, damage development, prevent investment and create further misery. Violence against ordinary citizens is inexcusable, and the onus is on the provincial authorities to ensure that those responsible are punished in accordance with the law. Beyond heightened security, vigilance and intelligence needs, lasting stability demands that the state assuage the political, economic and governance anxieties that fuel the cycle of violence. Matters have come to such a pass that without easing Balochistan’s sense of alienation through a complementary political effort, such tragedies will be hard to prevent. Counterterrorism actions, empathy for the people and dialogue with non-violent elements promise protection for all.

title: Maritime alliance
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AS the US-Iran war drags on, new battle lines are being drawn. The pro-US Gulf Arab monarchies and Iran have enjoyed a chequered history, specifically after the latter’s Islamic Revolution of 1979. But now, in the midst of the current conflict, the Arabs and Iranians are moving dangerously close to direct confrontation. One manifestation of this is the new maritime defence coalition that Saudi Arabia has just announced. At least 14 countries, among them Pakistan, Egypt and Turkiye, have signed a joint statement supporting the coalition that seeks to “strengthen maritime security” in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The development comes after the pro-Iran Yemeni Houthi militia announced a blockade of Saudi ports last month. Many saw the Houthi move as an Iranian pressure tactic to complement the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. While Tehran’s decision-makers may have sought to hurt the US and its allies with these closures, the truth is that they were affecting the entire international community, including some of Tehran’s own allies.
The result is that due to Iran’s hard line on Hormuz, and the Houthis’ move against the Saudis, Riyadh is developing a defence coalition apparently aimed at Iran and its allies. While Tehran’s mistrust of the US and Israel is understandable, its uncompromising posture is alienating many of its neighbours, and isolating it further. Much of the internal situation in Iran is the direct result of the US-Israeli aggression, as the more pragmatic figures have been assassinated, leaving relatively hard-line factions, such as the Pasdaran, to call the shots, especially in foreign policy. Those within the Iranian establishment who believe in maintaining better ties with their neighbours need to prevail on their compatriots, and rethink Tehran’s rigid approach.
It is evident that as the Iranians and Arabs move towards open confrontation, Israel is watching on with glee. During the Iran-Iraq war, then Israeli prime minister Menachem Begin was reported to have said that he wished “them both success”. One assumes the current Israeli regime has similar feelings towards the Arab-Iran stand-off. The situation demands wisdom and restraint from all sides. Once this war is over, America may leave, but the Arabs and Iranians have to live in the region. Hence, matters need to be addressed before they spiral out of control. The GCC and other Arab states and Iran must, among themselves, resolve to halt attacks on each other. Moreover, the Arabs should see to it that their soil is not used by foreign aggressors against Iran. Tehran, similarly, should ensure there is free passage for vessels through the region’s maritime chokepoints. Unless all sides show statesmanship, an ugly new chapter in this conflict is likely to open.

title: When AI commits suicide or kills us all!
author: M Zeb Khan
content:
There is a quiet but catastrophic crisis unfolding in the digital world - one not driven by rogue machines or science-fiction scenarios, but by something far more immediate: the collapse of trust. At the centre of it all is generative AI - tools that can produce startlingly realistic images, videos, voices and text. What started out as a novelty - a viral deepfake of a celebrity, a cloned voice prank, a synthetic political meme - has now begun to gnaw away at the very foundation of public life: our shared reality.

We are nearing a point where the boundary between the real and the artificial has all but disappeared. Videos of public figures making inflammatory statements, images of wars that never happened, synthetic voices delivering false confessions - none of this is theoretical. It is already here, and getting harder to detect. As AI-generated content becomes more convincing, the default human response will soon be suspicion, not trust. This creeping disillusionment is not just a cultural or ethical problem. It is essentially an existential problem for AI itself.

The power of AI - its promise in healthcare, education, journalism and governance - rests on a single, fragile foundation: the belief that what it produces can be trusted. But if AI becomes associated with deception and manipulation, if it becomes a synonym for disinformation, the public will reject it. This is not healthy skepticism. It's nihilism. It is the sense that "everything is fake, so nothing matters" - and it's particularly corrosive in democratic societies where shared facts are essential for informed debate and accountability. In that environment, trust becomes a casualty, and so does civil discourse.

If this trust collapses, AI would not be celebrated - it will be feared, regulated into a corner, or abandoned altogether in the public sphere. The companies building these tools may win short-term acclaim for technical brilliance, but they will lose the long game of social legitimacy. Ironically, this means that the greatest threat to AI is not political backlash or regulatory red tape. It is AI itself. That is why we must confront this issue head-on - with urgency and clarity.

First, AI-generated content must be clearly and indelibly marked. Whether it is a synthetic video, voice clip or image, it must carry a watermark - machine-detectable, permanent and tamper-proof. Not optional. Not buried in metadata. But embedded by design. This is technically possible but politicians, either unaware of the danger or reluctant to resist, hesitate to act.

Second, we need a global infrastructure for verification. Just as we have built institutions to monitor elections or nuclear material, we now need a robust, cross-border framework to authenticate digital content. Again, the tools exist. What is missing is political and industry will. Third, there must be real penalties for malicious deepfake deployment. Using AI to fabricate events, incite violence, discredit whistleblowers or manipulate elections must be treated as a serious criminal offence, not a clever use of technology.

Fourth, the public needs education in digital discernment. This is more than media literacy. It is reality literacy. People must be equipped to question what they see and hear - not to dismiss everything, but to navigate an information environment where deception can be indistinguishable from truth. And most importantly, AI companies must rethink their own trajectory. There is a false belief - especially in the tech world - that perfect realism is the ultimate goal. But if that realism leads to social collapse, if it destroys the possibility of verification, it is not innovation, it is self-sabotage.

AI does not have to be this way. We can still have synthetic content with ethical guardrails, intelligent systems that are powerful but accountable. But only if we act now, before cynicism becomes irreversible. Because the path we are on leads to a bleak paradox: the smarter AI becomes, the more damage it will do to the very conditions that make intelligence - human or artificial - worth having: trust, truth, and the capacity to engage with each other meaningfully. AI would not be destroyed by critics or regulation but by itself unless we stop it do so!

title: Local governance
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
INTERIOR Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s speech at a business summit on Thursday has stirred a hornet’s nest. His diagnosis that the present system of governance is collapsing is correct. His call for political parties to sit together and resolve the country’s issues is welcome — although it will depend on the extent to which the government is willing to engage opposition parties. His warning that business as usual will neither deliver prosperity, nor create jobs, nor fix governance failures is also timely. But his proposed cure — creating smaller provinces on administrative grounds — rests on the flawed assumption that such an exercise will automatically bring the government closer to citizens and resolve governance problems. This view is questionable. From time to time, different political parties, including the PPP, PML-N and MQM, have advocated new provinces for different reasons. Indeed, there is no harm in having a national debate to see whether a consensus can emerge. But it must be an inclusive, evidence-based and unrushed process, based on genuine and broad public participation. The exercise would require scrutiny inside and outside parliament, with a focus on economic viability, administrative capacity and resource distribution.
While the debate on new provinces should continue, there is a much simpler and more effective option available. The aims of devolution, better governance and administrative efficiency can be achieved by constitutionally guaranteeing the continuity of local governments as the effective third tier of governance at the centre and in the provinces. The issue is the failure to devolve political, administrative and financial authority to the local level, where public services are actually delivered. The problem is, no political party is prepared to empower elected LGs. That must change in order to facilitate decentralisation and good governance for a robust economy. New provinces were not the only governance reform the minister, who is considered close to the security establishment, appeared to advocate. He also, rather slyly, hinted at the ‘need’ to build support for an alternative system of governance within the democratic dispensation that would replace the existing federal parliamentary system. Given the serious internal and external threats facing the country, those in authority must refrain from making the parliamentary system, on which the nation has broadly agreed, contentious, as doing so would only strengthen divisive forces.
Published in Dawn, August 1st, 2026

title: Missing foundation of AI readiness
author: none@none.com (Asif Saad)
content:
ARTIFICIAL intelligence has quickly become a country, economy and boardroom priority. Across different organisations and industries, leaders are asking the same questions: which model should we use? Should we deploy ChatGPT or Claude? Do we need an AI strategy? Where should we begin? How quickly can we implement it? These are important questions. But I believe they overlook a more fundamental one: is our organisation actually ready to benefit from AI?
Over the last few months as I have been thinking about how AI is changing organisations, this question has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Many organisations are treating AI as a technology challenge when, in reality, it is exposing a much older management challenge. That cha­­llenge is how organisations manage information.
Most discussions assume that AI itself is the limiting factor. I suspect the opposite is true. For many organisations, particularly in developing economies like Pakistan, the limiting factor is the organisation itself.
    
Consider a manufacturing company operating several production lines. Every morning, the production manager decides which supervisors shou­­ld run which lines, which maintenance engineers should be assigned to planned shutdowns, which operators should work overtime and how production should be adjusted if a machine unexpectedly fails. These decisions rely on dozens of variables: employee skills and certifications, atte­n­dance, maintenance history, machine capability, quality performance, customer delivery commitments, inventory levels and production priorities. An AI system could analyse all these variables simultaneously and recommend the allocation most likely to maximise output, minimise downtime and meet customer commitments.
Two organisations can invest in the same AI technology and achieve different results.
Or take a call centre receiving thousands of calls each day. Traditionally, incoming calls are routed using simple rules such as the next available agent. An AI-enabled system, however, could optimise each interaction by simultaneously considering a far richer set of variables; the customer’s history and lifetime value, previous complaints, the complexity of the issue, the agent’s expertise, language proficiency, first-call resolution rate, customer satisfaction scores, current workload, average handling time and even the likelihood of customer churn.
Based on these factors, AI could assign each call to the agent most likely to resolve the issue quickly while maximising customer satisfaction and retention at the same time. But this capability depends on the availability of reliable organisational information. If customer histories are incomplete, agent skills are poorly documented, performance data is inaccurate or systems are disconnected, AI has little to optimise. It can only make better decisions when the organisation has already captured, maintained and integrated the information on which those decisions depend.
But there is one obvious question: from where does the AI obtain this information?
In many organisations, much of it does not exist in a form that AI can use. In my experience, working with different types of organisations, some information exists in an ERP system or other disconnected software. Some is stored in spreadsheets on individual laptops. A lot of it nowadays rests in WhatsApp conversations! And the most valuable knowledge frequently exists only in the minds of experienced managers.
Therefore, the production manager, not the organisation, knows which operator can recover a troubled production line, which maintenance engineer consistently diagnoses recurring faults and which supervisor performs best under pressure. The same with the call centre manager who relies on his personal knowledge of his teams’ capabilities to make critical decisions. This distinction is more significant than it first appears.
AI cannot optimise information that has never been captured, nor can it analyse knowledge that exists only in someone’s memory. Nor is it able to make better decisions when the underlying information is fragmented, inconsistent or inaccessible. In other words, it does not create organisational intelligence. It depends upon it.
This helps explain why two organisations can invest in the same AI technology and achieve completely different outcomes. One has spent years documenting processes, maintaining reliable operational data, integrating systems and making organisational knowledge accessible. The other relies on personal experience, informal processes and fragmented information. The technology is identical but the organisations are not.
For decades, experienced managers compensated for weak information systems. They knew where critical information was located, who possessed specialised expertise and how to make things happen despite organisational shortcomings. AI can’t be productive in the same way. It can only work with the information an organisation has chosen to capture, maintain and make ava­­ilable. This is why I believe we are asking the wrong question. Instead of asking whether organisations are adopting AI quickly enough, we should first ask whether they have built the organisational foundations that allow AI to create value.
That requires a different set of management questions. Where does our organisational knowledge reside? How much information exists only on individual laptops or in personal email folders or WhatsApp groups? Which decisions depend on a manager’s memory rather than organisational data? How reliable is our operational information? What information is continuously updated? And what information can AI actually access? These are not technology questions. They are management questions. This issue is particularly relevant for Pakistan. Many of our organisations have grown successfully despite fragmented information because capable managers developed ways to work around weak systems. But as AI becomes more deeply embedded in work, those workarounds become constraints.
The organisations that benefit most from AI are unlikely to be those that simply purchase the latest technology. They will be those that have invested in disciplined information, organised knowledge and management systems that make both available across the organisation.
Perhaps, then, the missing foundation of AI readiness is not more sophisticated technology, but greater organisational information maturity. That may ultimately prove to be AI’s most important lesson. Before AI can transform organisations, organisations must first transform the way they manage what they know.
The writer advises boards and CEOs on strategy, leadership and organisational transformation.

title: Resilience against organised crime
author: none@none.com (Tariq Parvez)
content:
IN recent years, Pakistan has taken many steps to combat organised crime (OC); resultantly, it was taken off the FATF grey list in 2022. However, it remains on the FATF’s ‘enhanced follow-up’ list in order to assess the sustained, on-the-ground implementation of its anti-money laundering/counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) steps.
Thus, our current status with the FATF requires us continuously to assess the implementation and effectiveness of our ongoing efforts against OC.
Tackling OC can be divided into two broad areas, ie, targeting criminality (criminal markets and actors) and strengthening society’s resilience against OC. While the first area focuses on intelligence, law enforcement and punitive measures, the second centres on addressing the contextual factors that provide an environment conducive to OC. This is the model followed by the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime in its successive Global Organised Crime Indices (GOCI). While not infallible, these global indices serve at least as rough-and-ready comparative assessments across different fields.
    
In its latest GOCI, issued in 2025, Pakistan has been placed in 45th position out of 193 countries, ie, in the category of countries with high vulnerability to OC and low resilience to combat it. That is a grave indictment of Pakistan’s efforts. It indicates that despite our ongoing policies, we not only remain extremely vulnerable to OC, but our will or capability to reduce the contextual factors sustaining it also remains very weak. This calls for a fundamental review of the balance between targeting criminality and strengthening resilience, which should complement each other.
Pakistan is among the countries with high vulnerability to organised crime — and low resilience against it.
While a lot has been written about efforts to deal with OC’s criminality (criminal markets and criminal actors), the subject of building resilience against OC in society has received little attention. GOCI 2025 has highlighted the following five areas of greatest weakness in building resilience against OC in Pakistan:
Political leadership and governance: The most important factor for building resilience against OC in any society is the quality of its political leadership and governance. Both these factors have been assessed by GOCI 2025 as having a non-existent or nominal role in building resilience in Pakistan. In fact, when political leadership and governance fail to play their due role, they not only facilitate OC but also weaken the government’s efforts to combat it. Four factors have been specifically identified in this regard. One, a lack of trust in state institutions because the controversial elections of 2024 weakened the government’s legitimacy. Two, political interference in law enforcement. Three, widespread corruption in the system. Four, the military’s retention of “substantial control over political processes”. It follows that improving the quality of political leadership and governance deserves the highest priority in building resilience against OC.
Judicial system and detention: The ability of any judicial system to dispense justice is crucial to building resilience against OC. Pakistan’s judiciary has been assessed by the indices as “weak and subject to political influence, with the military often shaping judicial outcomes”. Also, the latest Transparency International report has assessed the judiciary as the third most corrupt institution in the country. Working in such a judicial system makes combating OC difficult.
Government transparency and accountability: Countries with higher government transparency and greater accountability have been found to be more successful in combating OC. For Pakistan, the index has assessed both these factors as ineffective. The 2026 World Press Freedom Index has ranked Pakistan 153rd out of 180 countries — among the lowest 20 per cent in the world. In such an environment, it is risky for investigative journalists to publish reports about major scandals. Similarly, where accountability is concerned, organisations mandated to deal with corruption, like NAB, have been criticised “for political bias, often pursuing opposition leaders while protecting those aligned with the ruling establishment”. Interestingly, the 2025 Global Index on Fraud places Pakistan 112th out of 112 countries — in other words, it is the most permissive country in the world for fraudulent practices. OC thrives in such a society, and its main enablers continue largely unharmed, reducing the effectiveness of the law-enforcement agencies.
Economic regulatory capacity: Since OC is a form of criminal enterprise with the sole objective of making money through illegal activities economic regulatory institutions like SECP assume great importance. The GOCI ranks the capacity of Pakistan’s economic regulatory agencies very low. SECP’s recent initiative to develop a central registry of UBOs (ultimate beneficiary owners) this year is welcome. Its effectiveness on the ground, however, remains to be seen. There is a greater need for public scrutiny of agencies like SECP and for holding them accountable.
Victim and witness support: Another important pillar of the strategy to build resilience against OC is the extent of security provided to witnesses and victims of OC. In Pakistan, this is an example of technical compliance with FATF standards but with poor implementation. Every province has had specific witness protection laws for years; yet these laws have rarely been used and the witnesses have rarely been provided security, undermining the effectiveness of law-enforcement efforts and leading to non-reporting of OC and large-scale acquittals by the courts. The protection of witnesses needs to be given the importance it deserves.
The cumulative effect of the weaknesses of these five crucial areas is the creation of an environment conducive to the spread of OC. Combating OC in such a context is like fighting in hostile territory. The situation calls for national action plans by the AML authority in each of these five areas and regular monitoring with regard to specific key performance indicators. In the interest of transparency and accountability, the implementation reports of these action plans should be made public.
Strategically speaking, in the fight against OC, action against criminality and the effort to build resilience must go hand in hand. Ignoring one at the cost of the other is self-defeating. The sooner this is realised, the better it will be — otherwise, our successes shall continue to be merely tactical and the dents in OC shall remain superficial.
The writer is a former director general, Federal Investigation Agency, Pakistan.

title: Outsourcing as a policy
author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
content:
PUNJAB has outsourced some 18,000 primary schools to the private sector, with plans to outsource more schools. The government is also thinking about outsourcing middle and high schools as well as colleges. Will this momentum encompass universities? Let us wait and see.
The outsourcing ‘movement’ is not restricted to educational institutions. Punjab has been doing this in the health sector as well. And the federal government has been talking of airports and ports in this context. Other provinces are not far behind. Sindh has significant public-private partnerships in health. Moving forward, it seems the scope and intensity of outsourcing are likely to increase.
But what is the benefit of outsourcing? It should be remembered that educational institutions are run by governments across the world. We have excellent government-run schools in developed and rich countries as well as in developing and not-so-rich countries. Education is a public good and is usually provided, funded and managed by governments across the world. So, what is the advantage of outsourcing education? Why is this slowly becoming an article of faith in Punjab?
    
One argument that is given is that it is cheaper for the government to pay the private sector than to provide and manage education through its own department. Punjab was paying Rs800 or so to the private sector when its own per-child expenditure in public schools used to be roughly Rs2,500 per month.
The answer lies not in outsourcing but in improving the quality of service and governance.
A few caveats should be kept in mind. First, over time, the cost of providing education has gone up a lot and the government has had to move to about Rs1,500 per-child transfer as the private sector could not provide educational services at Rs800 per month. Punjab is now thinking of introducing an incentive structure for private-sector providers, and this might raise the average transfer to around Rs2,000. So, over time, the cost saving might diminish.
Second, the cost advantage is overstated. The education department outsourced the schools but did not have mechanisms for effectively regulating them. It is in the process of developing these systems. The latter will include periodic checks on enrolments and attendance, quality checks on teaching, testing students to obtain valid proof of performance, and checks on infrastructure and other services being provided. This will require quite an elaborate system; doing this for 18,000 schools spread across the province is not easy, and it will have certain costs as well. So, it is evident that per-child expenditure will go up significantly.
Third, and perhaps most importantly, the difference in per-child cost is reflected in what the private sector pays teachers compared with the salaries and benefits government teachers receive. Government salaries are more than the minimum wage (around Rs45,000 per month) — in fact, usually significantly above it. Government jobs come with job security, pensions, the right to leave and other benefits. The private sector, on the other hand, pays anywhere from around Rs8,000 to Rs25,000 per month to teachers. Rural low-fee schools are generally at the lower end. Even in low-fee urban schools, salaries are in the Rs10,000-Rs15,000 range. And there are no other benefits or job security in the private sector.
The government is currently taking advantage of the fact that it is not enforcing the minimum wage law in private-sector schools. This is the main source of savings for the government as it outsources schools. But this has medium- to long-term implications.
When 10-year agreements with private schools end, will all these government schools revert to their previous status? Or have they been outsourced forever? If the government takes them back, it will either need new teachers or have to absorb private-sector teachers as government employees. If the schools have been permanently outsourced, the contingent liability will be significant if the female labour market changes.
The private sector hires anyone who can teach. Sometimes teachers are graduates, but many times they hold only an Intermediate degree. The private sector provides very little teacher training and support and has to deal with high teacher turnover as well. Will this help with the quality of education and improve learning outcomes? There will be implications for both the teacher labour market and teaching as a profession. On the one hand, governments want teachers to be professional (Sindh has introduced teacher licensing). On the other hand, outsourcing is making the teacher market more informal and unstructured. If salaries are around Rs20,000 or less, who in their right mind would want to choose teaching as a profession? Outsourcing and teacher professionalisation seem to be at odds, especially if the idea is to exploit cheap female labour for teaching.
Another argument given for outsourcing is that this government is not able to run schools and the private sector does it better. But this is just a poor argument. Governments run schools all over the world. If this is specific to Pakistan, does the government do a better job at policing and providing justice and security? If not, should these functions also be outsourced? Clearly not. The answer lies not in outsourcing but in improving the quality of service and governance.
The mantra of outsourcing is all the rage these days, especially in Punjab. And leading this momentum is education. With some 18,000 schools already outsourced, the initiative is no longer a pilot or a policy in the making. But the arguments for outsourcing seem weak. The cost advantage is overstated; the salary differential is not. However, relying on lower salaries will have significant medium- to long-term impacts on teacher labour markets and the teaching profession. The argument that the government is unable to manage schools or govern effectively stems from laziness and is a very lame excuse. Once the rage subsides, one hopes we will have time to evaluate the policy and its outcomes rigorously and to course-correct accordingly.
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
Published in Dawn, July 31st, 2026

title: Unfair tax system
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE disclosure that the FBR collected nearly Rs1.9tr in sales and income taxes through electricity bills over the past four years is hardly a matter of pride. Indeed, it shows that the tax system has come to depend on extracting ever more money from those it can easily reach rather than bringing the vast number of untaxed into the net. The revelation that Rs400bn to 500bn in adjustable income tax withholding goes unclaimed annually further exposes the system’s flaws: those outside the formal tax net are content with paying indirect taxes rather than entering the tax system, while those not liable to pay taxes keep bearing the burden because the state has chosen the easiest point of collection. The cumulative burden of electricity consumption and income taxes falls disproportionately on ordinary households.
The FBR chairman told a parliamentary panel recently that the sales tax bill included ‘normal sales tax, extra tax, further tax and tax on electricity supplied to retailers’. Income tax, meanwhile, was withheld from industrial and commercial consumers and even domestic consumers. He warned that electricity could face more taxes, arguing that it receives the highest concessions. But how much more can consumers be expected to bear? Electricity bills are already burdened with high tariffs, debt and other surcharges, fuel adjustments and an array of levies. A panel member rightly described tax collection through electricity bills as “tantamount to coercion”. That the state is using electricity bills as a convenient collection mechanism means it is effectively forcing millions to pay taxes before establishing whether they are actually liable to do so. This is hardly sound fiscal policy. Nor is it sustainable. The failure lies in the state’s approach to taxation. Revenue collection has become an end in itself, while the more difficult task of broadening the tax base is repeatedly postponed. A state that cannot distinguish between a taxable citizen and a non-taxable consumer is making taxation more coercive.

title: Indus unites
author: none@none.com (Hassan Abbas)
content:
FOR over 6,000 years, the Indus was the spine of one of the world’s earliest urban civilisations. At Mohenjodaro and Harappa, archaeologists found planned cities, drains, granaries and markets, but no weapons or fortresses. The Indus people built baths, docks and trade links to Mesopotamia and the Gulf. The river was their road. It carried cargo, ideas and people, stitching communities together instead of dividing them.
The shift began in the 1850s. After annexing Punjab, the British built the Bari Doab and Sirhind Canals to settle soldiers and reward allies. These colonial projects diverted water politically, creating the first water conflicts and pitting upstream and downstream communities against each other instead of promoting cooperation.
After 1947, India and Pakistan continued British policies, dividing and damming the Indus for short-term political goals without a basin-wide vision. This created a ‘robbing Peter to pay Paul’ system. The delta lost fresh flows and silt. Canal areas got water but faced waterlogging, salinity and feuds over water rights. Both lack clean water and dignity. Debt grew despite billions spent, while we clung to a colonial irrigation model built for an empire, not a nation.
After air, water is the most basic need of life. But water also has a second nature. When it is allowed to flow, it connects. When it is dammed and diverted, it divides. To reverse this, Pakistan needs to invoke the grand economic engine that has united regions elsewhere: inland navigation. China’s Grand Canal, built over 1,400 years, kept north and south economically linked and politically united. The 1825 Erie Canal cut freight costs by 90 per cent, connecting the Midwest to New York. The 1992 Danube-Rhine corridor turned European rivals into partners by giving 11 nations a shared stake in one navigable river. Each linked sea trade to inland waterways, delivering cheaper goods, integrated markets and greater peace.
Water connects when allowed to flow.
The Indus offers the same possibility on a larger scale. From Karachi on the Arabian Sea, the Indus and its five tributaries form a 3,200-kilometre network reaching every major Pakistani city. Barges of 500 to 1,000 tons could run from Karachi to Hyderabad, Sukkur, D.G. Khan, Mianwali, Attock and Peshawar, with feeders linking Multan, Bahawalpur, Lahore, Faisalabad and Sialkot. Karachi could become South Asia’s Rotterdam. Freight costs from Punjab to port could fall sharply, while solar-powered barges would save billions in fuel and carbon emissions.
But the true power of navigation is not economic. It is diplomatic. The Indus is the only natural corridor from the heart of Asia to the seafaring trade. If we develop it, we can offer Afghanistan a direct link to the seafaring world. A navigable channel up the Indus and then up the Kabul River to Jalalabad would give landlocked Afghan­istan a port. In return, Pakistan gains transit revenue and a neighbour whose prosperity depends on a stable river system.
The same logic extends east. The Ravi and Sutlej flow into Pakistan. With free flowing rivers, barges from Gurdaspur and Ferozepur in Indian Punjab could also reach the Arabian Sea through Pakistan. This is exactly how the Danube and Rhine forced European states to cooperate after centuries of war. When upstream and downstream both need the channel to stay open, they would jointly agree on free flow and pollution control. Water stops being a zero-sum resource and becomes a shared asset.
Extending north and west, the Indus can connect even more. Cargo from Central Asia could travel down the Panj and Kabul rivers to Jalalabad, then by barge to Karachi, cutting sea access distance in half versus routes through Iran or the Black Sea. Goods from Xinjiang could descend via the Karakoram to Gilgit and then by river. For the first time, the world’s largest landlocked region would gain a direct, low-cost route to the ocean, turning fragmented areas into one economic space, like China’s Grand Canal did.
To make this work, we must change how we manage the river. We divert 100 MAF for irrigation, but lose 50pc in canals and 30pc to flood irrigation. Switching to piped, pressurised supply from riverine wells could cut use to 20-25 MAF and boost yields, freeing over 75 MAF — over 10 times Tarbela’s storage. Flowing rivers would recharge aquifers, restore forests, enable navigation, and end feuds. The rural peace dividend alone would be worth billions. This vision needs new priorities: clean water first, efficient irrigation second, flowing rivers third. It means solar power for pumps and barges, pollution controls, and investment in locks and ports.
We can continue the 1850s path, or return to Mohenjodaro’s logic. Indus unites, not divides. When a river flows for everyone, everyone prospers.
The writer has a PhD in hydrology and water resources from Michigan State University.

title: Drowning the future
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
THE floods are visiting us again. The death toll will be counted within days. The damage to roads, bridges and embankments will be tallied within weeks and translated into a dollar figure. Expect this assessment to dominate the coverage. It is legitimate but a wrong ledger regardless. The real casualty of this flood, and the one before it, and the one before that, is not standing in the rubble. It is sitting in a classroom that no longer exists, or should be sitting there and is not.
Pakistan is a country where 40 per cent of the population is under 15, where 93 million children are of school age, where the state has for years spent less than one per cent of GDP on health and less than 2pc on education despite disasters. When the water recedes, the roads get rebuilt. The child who missed seven weeks of school, who was screened for severe acute malnutrition at a flood clinic, who caught malaria from a collapsed WASH system, does not get rebuilt on the same timeline. Evidence from the 2005 earthquake shows four weeks of closure can cost a child one and a half years of learning four years later. Pakistan has just handed its children five years of near continuous disruption: Covid, the 2022 floods, the 2024 heatwaves, the 2025 floods. Each calamity more severe than the last.
    
Before the 2022 floods, 26.2m children were already out of school, the second highest figure in the world. The floods destroyed or damaged 27,000 schools, converted 5,000 more into relief camps, and locked 3.5m children out of learning in a single season. By January 2023, only 200,000 had received any education intervention. The provincial numbers show that the out-of-school share jumped from 32 to 80pc in Khairpur Mirs and from 46 to 86pc in Jacobabad. Entire districts where enrolment simply stopped. The pattern held: 1,300 more schools damaged in 2024, 230,000 children in Sindh losing access, nearly 30,000 schools damaged in Punjab in 2025, affecting 700,000 more. Each cycle adds to the base rather than starting from zero. Displaced teachers, especially women, do not return to classrooms that no longer exist. The system absorbs the loss quietly, without a ledger.
    
Girls absorb this collapse first and hardest. Even before 2022, the out-of-school rate for girls aged five to 16 stood at 59pc in Balochistan and 51pc in Sindh. When a flood or a drought strips a household of income, a daughter’s schooling is usually the first expense cut, and marriage becomes a coping strategy. The 2022 floods alone are linked to an 18pc rise in child marriage prevalence — five years of progress erased in a single monsoon. The term now in the literature is ‘monsoon brides’. Researchers have traced the chain across South Asia: economic shock triggers withdrawal from school, withdrawal triggers marriage, and marriage closes the door on everything meant to follow. This is a girl absent from every flood damage assessment. The floodwaters recede but they leave monsoon brides behind.
Pakistan has handed its children five years of near continuous disruption.
The harm does not stop at school gates or wedding registers. After the 2022 floods, half of the 3.4m children needing assistance showed signs of psychological distress, and seven in 10 Sindh parents reported depressive symptoms in their children. Pakistan has no framework to recognise this as loss, no methodology to measure it, no mechanism to compensate for it.
The same demographic pressure that turns a flood into a generational event turns a heatwave into one too. Global tracking shows infants and children under five now experience more heatwave days per year than any other age group, a fourfold increase over two decades, and Pakistan’s heatwaves already exceed 50 degrees Celsius. In 2024, that exposure alone shuttered classrooms for roughly half of all school-age children. Unicef’s 2026 Children’s Climate Risk Report has found that 1.1 billion of the world’s children are now exposed to three or more climate hazards simultaneously, and named Pakistan among the countries most severely affected. We can layer this onto a country ranked 109th of 127 nations on the Global Hunger Index, where up to 40pc of children under five are stunted and a third of mothers are malnourished. A child entering a heatwave, drought or a flood in Pakistan is not entering it from a healthy baseline. He is already behind, and the event does not reset him to zero, it pushes him further back.
    
Pakistan cannot see the scale of what it is losing, because it is not counting it. None of the official estimates, including the 2022 Post-Disaster Needs Assessment or the 2026 lessons-learned reviews, has counted it. Child deaths from malaria, cholera and respiratory illness after floods are rarely registered and are thus invisible to policymakers. Regional modelling projects that sustained climate-related learning disruption could generate up to $380bn in lost future earnings by 2050, a figure absent from our projections. This is what the country loses when it fails to protect the children who are supposed to grow into its workforce, tax base and its institutions.
The way forward has to run in the same sequence as the damage, not around it. First, disaster relief funds need a mandatory child impact reporting requirement, tracking school closures, malnutrition screening, child marriage referrals and mortality alongside infrastructure damage, published on the same timeline as the damage assessment. Second, education recovery financing needs to be pre-positioned rather than requested after each disaster, a drawdown facility that can disburse within weeks and carries a funded protocol for keeping girls enrolled once household income collapses. Third, Pakistan needs to bring its own child climate risk data into climate finance negotiations, rather than relying on an external index to describe a crisis the state has not measured for itself.
Pakistan does not lack evidence of what is happening to its children. It lacks a mechanism, in its own data systems and in the loss and damage registry, to make that harm count.
This article draws on a talk by the writer last month at the University College London-Unicef Roundtable, London Climate Action Week.
Published in Dawn, July 30th, 2026

title: End trafficking
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
MODERN slavery, in the form of human trafficking, is among the state’s gravest failures. Scores of Pakistanis are trafficked annually, yet the conviction rate for those who traffick them remains low. This World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, under the theme ‘Trapped behind a scam’, focuses on the rising “form of trafficking in persons for forced criminality”. It is linked to financial scams, corruption, money-laundering and cybercrime. The UN drugs and crime agency says that, at present, over 300,000 people are stuck in Southeast Asia’s scam centres. While the region has long been a hub of the menace, the extent of the criminal network became apparent last year when victims from 80 countries were identified. UNODC wants more measures, including cross-border judicial and law-enforcement support, to protect victims and dismantle transnational crime rings.
Human traffickers thrive amidst conflict and socioeconomic despair. Desperate people fall for fake job offers placed through ‘legal’ companies, followed by ‘professional’ interviews and contracts. But their destination is a cruel scam compound where they face isolation, threats, debt bondage, torture and sexual abuse. Pakistan should take this as a warning, and collaborate with Bangladesh, the Maldives and Sri Lanka in their attempts to end this kind of trafficking. For this, it is essential for the state to accept that a culture of impunity is forcing the poor out. Besides the lack of job opportunities, corrupt officers, legal loopholes, political patronage and weak enforcement of the Prevention of Trafficking in Persons Act, 2018, and the Prevention of Smuggling of Migrants Act, 2018, create miserable conditions. The need for reforms is dire, as is the training and resourcing of security forces — all focused on victim safety and rehabilitation. The brutality of human trade does not invite public outrage because the government has been unsuccessful in raising awareness. As a result, the country has compromised cititzens’ safety and diminished its international image.
Published in Dawn, July 30th, 2026
